summary: This bill amends the tax code to let beneficiaries withdraw up to $35,000 tax-free from a 529 plan held for 15+ years and use it within 60 days to buy their first home, with recapture if the home is sold within five years.

scores.thoughts: The bill amends the tax code to permit tax-free distributions from 529 plans for home purchases. It contains no appropriations, direct outlays, or changes to federal spending programs, so it has no bearing on government spending levels.

The core provision expands the tax-free uses of qualified tuition programs (529 plans) by allowing up to $35,000 in long-term contributions and earnings to be withdrawn without tax penalty for first-time home purchases. This directly reduces the tax burden on those specific distributions, constituting a targeted tax benefit.
No provisions address health insurance, medical care delivery, public health programs, or related tax treatment.
No provisions relate to firearms, background checks, or gun regulations.
No provisions address immigration status, visas, border policy, or pathways to citizenship.
No provisions address reproductive health services or abortion access.
No provisions address military budgets, defense procurement, or national security spending.
No provisions address environmental regulations, emissions standards, or conservation programs.
No provisions modify welfare programs, SNAP, housing vouchers, or other safety-net entitlements.

The bill permits diversion of funds from 529 education savings plans to home purchases. While this touches education-focused tax-advantaged accounts, it does not alter public school funding, federal education policy, or school choice mechanisms, making the connection tangential at best.
No provisions address drug enforcement, decriminalization, or substance abuse programs.
No provisions address sentencing, policing, incarceration, or criminal justice reform.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, or import/export policy.

By expanding tax-free distributions, the bill forgoes potential tax revenue. This has a minor, indirect effect on the deficit but does not establish any debt-reduction target or new deficit-financed program.
No provisions address legal protections or rights for LGBTQ+ individuals.
No provisions address foreign assistance, international aid, or State Department funding.
No provisions address voting access, election administration, or campaign finance.
No provisions address data privacy, technology regulation, or surveillance policy.
No provisions address collective bargaining, worker protections, or union rules.
No provisions address religious exemptions or anti-discrimination laws.
